title: Loneliness
hook: God sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, cast your care: a throwing word, and Hannah eating her dinner before anything had changed. Your line was he cares for you. When the worry came back, did you throw it again? Day one thousand four hundred.

Early in Genesis, before anything has gone wrong, before a single bite of fruit, God looks at something and calls it not good. It isn't a sin. It's a man by himself. "It is not good that the man should be alone." Loneliness is there in the Bible's opening pages, named by God himself as a problem. And it's still here. An apartment where the only voice is the television. A crowded dorm and nobody to call. A kitchen table set for one after years of setting it for two. Today: loneliness.

Start with the psalm. Psalm 68 says, in the King James words: "God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains." Look at who stands next to whom. The solitary, beside the prisoners. The psalm treats loneliness as a kind of captivity, and God as the one who opens the door and walks people into a home. Next, Jesus widens what family means. In Mark, someone tells him his mother and brothers are outside asking for him. He looks around at the people sitting in a circle with him and says: "Behold my mother and my brethren! For whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and mother." A family you can be set into, not only born into. Then the cross, in John's Gospel. Jesus is dying, and his mother is standing there with the disciple he loved. He says to her, "Woman, behold thy son!" And to the disciple, "Behold thy mother!" Then the text adds: "And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home." Even then, he makes sure she won't be left alone. The psalm's promise, done in two sentences. Last, Jesus in the garden. In Gethsemane he asks Peter and two others to stay awake with him, and finds them sleeping: "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" So loneliness, in these texts, isn't a failure of faith. Jesus himself asked for company and found his friends asleep. And the setting-in, the psalm's promise, often arrives through a person: someone who calls, who knocks, who takes another person home.

Here's the practice: contact someone lonely. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who might be lonely right now: a neighbor who lost a spouse, a friend who moved away, a coworker who eats lunch alone, a relative nobody calls much anymore. Let one face come clearly. Picture where they are at this moment, what the room around them looks like. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. Then decide what you'll do after the bell: a text, a call, a knock on a door. Keep it small enough that you'll really do it. The bell holds the time.
Loneliness. Being alone when you don't want to be. Genesis calls it not good, and Psalm 68 says God sets the solitary in families.

Your line: set in families. Today, make that call or send that text, and be for one person the family they're set into. This week ran from the church doing wrong, through church hurt, hypocrites, wounded healers, fear not and cast your care. It ends with a door opening. Day one thousand four hundred.

howItsDone: Christians care for lonely people through home visits, bringing communion to people who can't leave home, shared meals after services, and small groups; some churches keep lists of members to call or visit regularly.

original.note: Hebrew: the solitary ones, people on their own — the word in Psalm 68:6 (68:7 in Hebrew Bibles).

trapdoor: what you thought: being lonely means your faith is weak.
what it means: Genesis calls aloneness not good, Jesus felt it in Gethsemane, and Psalm 68 says God sets the solitary in families.
what a scholar hears: in Psalm 68 the solitary stand beside those bound with chains. loneliness pictured as a captivity, and God opening the door.

notes: Mark 3:31–35 is sometimes read as tension with Jesus's family; the lesson presents it only as widening family, without commenting on his relatives. Confirm.
'The psalm treats loneliness as a kind of captivity' is an interpretive reading of the pairing in Psalm 68:6; confirm or soften.
Original: יְחִידִים in Psalm 68:7 (Hebrew numbering); the KJV 'in families' renders a Hebrew phrase closer to 'in a home'. The lesson doesn't build on this. Confirm spelling.
